===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a polished, fully offline iOS trip-planning app called "Waypoint".
Native Apple stack only: SwiftUI + SwiftData for persistence, MapKit for
all mapping, ActivityKit for Live Activities, EventKit for calendar
export. No backend, no accounts, no third-party SDKs, no network calls
except on-device MapKit/local geocoding (which works offline-cached but
may need network for tile fetch — if a feature would require live
network for correctness, don't fake it; record it as a gap). Follow the
ios-app-factory-rules.

Core features (complete over broad — ship fewer things fully working):

1. Trips & itinerary: create trips with a date range; each trip has
   multiple days; each day has an ordered list of stops (place name,
   address, optional MapKit-resolved coordinate, time window, notes,
   category icon). Reorder stops via drag-and-drop within a day AND
   across days. Get date math right across the trip's date range,
   including a trip that starts and ends on the same day and a
   single-day trip.

2. Map view: a MapKit view per day showing all of that day's stops as
   annotations connected by a route line (MKDirections walking/driving,
   gracefully degrading to a straight-line polyline with a visible
   "approximate" indicator if MKDirections has no network). Tapping a
   stop centers the map and highlights it; tapping a map pin selects
   the corresponding itinerary row (two-way binding).

3. Expense splitting: a per-trip list of travelers (name, no accounts).
   Log expenses (amount, payer, split method: equal / exact amounts /
   percentage) against any subset of travelers. A settle-up screen
   computing the minimum set of payments to zero every balance (the
   classic debt-simplification graph problem — get this genuinely
   correct, including rounding remainders so amounts always sum
   exactly). Use Decimal, never Double, for money.

4. Packing lists: per-trip checklist, templates the user can save and
   reapply to future trips, a "packed %" indicator.

5. Live Activity: while a trip is "active" (today falls within its date
   range), a Live Activity / Dynamic Island showing the current or next
   stop and time until it, updating as stops are checked off. Must
   degrade gracefully (no crash, no Live Activity) on devices/OS
   versions without support, and when the user denies the permission.

6. Calendar export: export a day's stops as EventKit calendar events
   (with the user's explicit permission), one event per stop honoring
   its time window; must not create duplicate events if exported twice
   for the same day — detect and either skip or update existing ones.

7. Home-screen widget (WidgetKit, separate target): shows the active
   trip's next stop, or "no active trip" honestly if none.

8. iPad: itinerary list and map must work as a genuine two-column split
   view on iPad, not just a stretched phone layout.

Priorities: the debt-simplification math, the drag-reorder data
integrity (no duplicate/lost stops across days), and honest degradation
of every system-permission-gated feature (Live Activities, Calendar,
location) — never fake success when a permission is denied or a
capability is unavailable in the Simulator. Explicitly call out in a
Gaps section anything requiring infrastructure this project can't
provide (live traffic data, real-time flight tracking, iCloud trip
sync). Seed a "demo trip" toggle in Settings with realistic multi-day
sample data so no screen is empty on first review. Provide a clear way
to run it in the iOS Simulator via Xcode.

I want to push on the seams that haven't actually been nailed down yet, even though a lot of the hard math and permission-degradation stuff is already locked from earlier phases.

First, trip date-range editing after stops already exist. Nobody's said what happens when a user creates a 5-day trip, adds stops to day 4, then edits the trip to be 3 days. Do those day-4 stops get deleted, silently orphaned, or does the app refuse to shrink the range while stops exist on the trimmed days? This is the same category of bug as the drag-integrity problem everyone's worried about, just triggered by trip editing instead of dragging, and if it's not decided now it'll get built as an afterthought — probably as a silent cascade delete, which is a real data-loss risk nobody consented to. I'd resolve this now: shrinking a trip's date range that would orphan stops on removed days must block the edit and surface exactly which days/stops are affected, forcing the user to move or delete those stops first. Extending the range is trivially safe and needs no gate.

Second, the percentage-split remainder rule only covers rounding cents, not the case where user-entered percentages don't sum to 100 at all (which product_research explicitly flagged as an adversarial test case but never resolved into a UI/data rule). Does the app auto-scale entered percentages proportionally to sum to 100, reject the expense with a validation error, or store it as entered and let the imbalance flow into settle-up? These produce different settle-up totals for the same input, so this needs one deterministic answer, not "the algorithm should be smart about it." My vote: reject at entry time with a clear inline error ("percentages sum to 97%, add 3% somewhere") rather than silently rescaling, because silent rescaling is exactly the kind of "quiet reinterpretation of what the user typed" that violates the honesty principle already established for this app.

Third, drag-and-drop reordering has no accessible alternative on the table anywhere in this thread. VoiceOver users cannot perform a drag gesture reliably, and Apple's own HIG treats this as a real access requirement, not a nice-to-have. If the entire cross-day integrity guarantee is only exercised through a drag gesture, this app is unusable for a chunk of users and untestable by non-visual means. There needs to be a parallel "Move to..." action (context menu or edit-mode button) that goes through the exact same atomic SwiftData operation as the drag path — not a second, divergent code path that could reintroduce the duplication bug everyone's so focused on preventing in the gesture-based path.

Fourth, the demo-trip toggle's actual state machine has a gap: what happens on repeated on/off/on toggling? If toggling on always inserts a fresh demo trip, toggling it off and back on twice creates two demo trips, which is either confusing or a subtle duplication bug hiding behind a "feature." I'd lock this as: the demo trip is a singleton keyed by a stable identifier; toggling on either creates it if absent or does nothing if present; toggling off deletes that exact trip and nothing else (never touches real user trips even if their names or dates coincidentally overlap).

## StoreKit 2 — In-App Purchase & Subscriptions

**Use it when:** you sell anything — consumables, non-consumables, or auto-renewable subscriptions. Replaces callback-based StoreKit 1 entirely.

**Start from:** `Product` (fetch + purchase) and `Transaction` (entitlements + history). No server strictly required — signatures are verified on-device via `VerificationResult`.

### The three things you must do

1. **Load products by ID** (IDs come from App Store Connect):

```swift
func purchase(_ product: Product) async throws -> Transaction? {
    let result = try await product.purchase()
    switch result {
    case .success(let verification):
        let transaction = try checkVerified(verification)
        await transaction.finish()          // REQUIRED — unfinished txns replay forever
        return transaction
    case .userCancelled, .pending:
        return nil
    @unknown default:
        return nil
    }
}

func checkVerified<T>(_ result: VerificationResult<T>) throws -> T {
    switch result {
    case .unverified(_, let error): throw error   // signature failed — do NOT grant
    case .verified(let safe):       return safe
    }
}

The original prompt names eight features as core, but "complete over broad" is the explicit instruction, and prior phases already sequenced trips/reorder/settlement first, calendar/iPad second, Live Activity/widget last — so I want this phase's must-have list to be narrower than "all eight," with the difference between must and should driven by which failures are actually catastrophic to the app's trust pitch versus which are just missing polish.

My must-have list, and the reason each one is non-negotiable rather than aspirational: trip creation with correct date-range math including single-day and same-start/end-day trips, because getting this wrong breaks every downstream day/stop computation silently; the day view with ordered, timed stops; drag-reorder within and across days implemented as one atomic SwiftData operation, plus the non-gesture "Move to..." path through that same operation, because a duplicated or orphaned stop is the single worst thing this app could do and accessibility can't be an afterthought bolted on later; the per-day map view with MKDirections routing and a visibly labeled approximate-line fallback, with two-way tap selection between pin and list row; the traveler list and expense entry across all three split methods with percentage-sum validation rejecting non-100% entries inline; the settle-up screen running genuine minimum-transaction debt-simplification with Decimal math, payer-absorbs-remainder rounding, and an in-code sum-identity assertion; the trip date-range shrink guard that blocks edits which would orphan stops and names which ones; and the demo-trip singleton toggle with its visible Demo marker and at least one deliberately unresolvable-route stop. I'd also put a general "honest degradation" requirement in the must list as its own line item, not folded into individual features — every permission-gated capability (Live Activity, Calendar, location/MapKit network) must have an observably correct denied/unavailable state, because this is the thing most likely to get "coded defensively but never actually watched failing" if it's not called out as its own acceptance bar.

Where I'd push back against my own instinct to be maximally conservative: packing lists and calendar export are explicitly named core features in the prompt (4 and 6), so I don't think I can honestly demote them to should without contradicting the prompt directly — but I'd split them internally. Packing checklist plus packed-percentage is must-have (it's a simple per-trip list, low risk, cheap to get right); packing templates (save/reapply across trips) is should, because template reuse implies a second data model (template vs instance) that's easy to get subtly wrong under time pressure and isn't required for the app to be honest or useful on a single trip. Calendar export itself is must-have given it's explicitly named and has a fully-specified dedup mechanism already locked (stored EventKit identifier, lookup-and-update, explicit handling of revoked permission or externally-deleted events) — there's no ambiguity left blocking it, so demoting it would be avoiding a solved problem, not a risk-based cut. iPad split view I'd also keep as must, since it's explicitly named, already has a locked verification bar (independent two-pane behavior across sizes/orientations, not just NavigationSplitView), and doesn't carry the same "can't verify in Simulator" risk that Live Activity does.

Live Activity and the home-screen widget I'd keep as should, not must, and this is the one place I'd actually diverge from treating "named in the prompt" as automatically must-have: both carry a verification ceiling that's already been named twice in this project (Dynamic Island rendering and widget refresh timing can't be conclusively confirmed outside physical hardware), both must degrade to "no crash, no Live Activity / honest no-active-trip" on unsupported devices or denied permission, and if build time runs short, shipping a smaller finished app without them is explicitly preferred over a half-verified Live Activity that nobody can actually confirm behaves correctly in review. StoreKit/Pro-tier gating, the Trip Snapshot export, and the settlement audit-log/category-spend reporting are could-haves for this build — they're monetization and reporting layers on top of an already-correct free experience, not things the core promise depends on, and per_app_product_brief already treats the audit-log feature as conceptually agreed but undesigned.

Won't-build, explicitly: CloudKit/iCloud sync of any kind, any AirDrop/share-sheet mechanism that resembles live sync, real-time traffic/flight/weather data, cross-device collaborative editing, and destination-timezone-aware itineraries (stop times are local-device-timezone only, per the locked Gap). These need to survive into the final output as a named Gaps section, not just an absence — a reviewer should see them called out, not discover them by their absence.

The single biggest risk to my own framework: if Live Activity and widget end up should-have and get cut under time pressure, the app still ships a fully honest, fully correct core experience — but if packing templates or calendar export get cut instead because they "feel" similar in difficulty, that would violate the prompt's explicit feature list without the same verification-ceiling justification I'm using for Live Activity/widget. Whatever final MoSCoW table comes out of this phase needs to preserve that distinction — not all "cut under pressure" candidates are equally justified, and the justification has to be about unverifiable capability ceilings, not just "this looked hard."
